title: What is Norfolk's plan to protect the city from coastal storm flooding (the floodwall project), and how far along is it?
summary: What the records show as of November 16, 2026 about Resilient Norfolk, the Coastal Storm Risk Management (CSRM) project the City is building with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. The City's project page says Congress authorized it in 2020, that under the Corps' January 2022 infrastructure-law plan the City will receive $399,331,000, and that it has four phases: a floodwall and levees around downtown (Phase 1, split into 1A to 1D) and protection for the Pretty Lake, Lafayette River and Broad Creek areas, plus a voluntary Nonstructural Program that elevates or floodproofs individual buildings. WHRO reported that Council approved the partnership agreement with the Corps in April 2023, with the federal government paying 65% and Norfolk just over $931 million, and that City staff called that obligation daunting. The adopted FY 2027-2031 capital plan shows $159.2 million appropriated to date ($126.2 million of it general capital, the rest water and wastewater utility money), $25 million for FY 2027 (anticipated state grant money) and $6.2 million for FY 2028, and says the City's ability to pay its match depends on the state; the City reported a $25 million state Community Flood Preparedness Fund grant in April 2026. Council has since approved a right of entry for the Corps to investigate City land for the downtown wall (September 2025), a design-build contract for the Nonstructural Program (April 2026; about 1,000 pre-eligible buildings, with welcome letters sent to Tier 1 owners in February 2026), and an $85,000 review agreement with Norfolk Southern for a flood gate across its tracks near Lamberts Point (June 2026). WHRO reported on November 12, 2026 that first-phase sitework is underway with wall construction set for 2027, and that Council unanimously approved a $1.5 million study with the Corps of coastal protections for Southside communities, which WHRO reported in July 2025 the current design leaves with home elevations but no wall. What isn't settled: WHRO reported in 2025 that the cost is expected to rise beyond the $2.6 billion Congress approved and the finish date moved to 2037, and that the City asked to move the wall's path along the Freemason waterfront, which the City's chief resilience officer said requires federal authorization. WHRO also reported that the Southside study agreement doesn't mention the local stormwater drainage that flooded underpasses on August 4, 2026. City Council approves the City's agreements for the project.

what_would_help.text: Watch Council's agendas for the Southside study agreement's text (not yet posted on the meeting portal) and for any revised cost estimate or change to the Freemason alignment, which WHRO reports need federal approval.

The City's share depends on state support: the adopted capital plan says so, and the FY 2027 money is an anticipated state grant. The state's Community Flood Preparedness Fund has already granted the City $25 million for the project; watch for further state awards.
Owners of buildings that may be pre-eligible for elevation, basement fill or floodproofing can check with the Office of Resilience; the program is voluntary and enrolls in tiers.

For street and underpass flooding from heavy rain, also look at the stormwater projects in the capital plan: WHRO reports the new Southside study agreement doesn't mention local stormwater drainage, which flooded the underpasses in August 2026.
